entries.meaning: At Rama's arrival Mount Pravarshana's flowering forest becomes abundant and auspicious; gods, siddhas, and sages serve him in the forms of bees, birds, and deer. Rama and Lakshmana sit on a bright crystal slab discussing devotion, dispassion, statecraft, and discernment. As the monsoon clouds gather, Rama likens dancing peacocks to a detached householder rejoicing on meeting a devotee of Vishnu.

Rama reads the monsoon as moral imagery: proud clouds thunder while separation makes his heart afraid; lightning's brief flash resembles a wicked person's unstable affection; rain-clouds bow near earth as the learned become humble; mountains bear raindrops as saints bear abuse. Mud resembles maya clinging to a being, lakes gather water as virtues gather in the good, and rivers become still in the ocean as a soul rests on finding Hari. Grass-hidden paths resemble true scriptures obscured by sectarian argument.

Frogs sound like students reciting the Veda; trees put out new leaves like an aspirant's mind gaining discernment, while useless plants lose their leaves as wicked schemes fail under good rule. Crops, fireflies, broken field-ridges, weeding farmers, vanished chakravakas, barren soil, multiplying creatures, and resting travellers each become moral analogies. Winds scatter clouds like a bad son destroying family virtue; daylight alternates between darkness and sun as knowledge perishes through bad company and arises through good company.

The rains pass and beautiful autumn arrives. White kans-grass displays the monsoon's old age; rising Agastya dries road-water as contentment dries greed. Clear rivers and lakes resemble saints free of pride and delusion, and their gradually receding water resembles the wise relinquishing possessiveness. Wagtails return in season like timely good deeds; fish suffer as water shrinks, like an improvident householder without wealth. Clear sky resembles a devotee who has abandoned every other hope, and a rare autumn shower resembles the rare person who attains Rama's devotion.

Fish in deep water are happy like those sheltered by Hari; lotus-filled lakes resemble attributeless Brahman made manifest with attributes. Bees and birds sound, while the chakravaka grieves at night like a wicked person seeing another's prosperity, and the thirsty chataka resembles one hostile to Shiva who finds no happiness. Moonlight removes autumn heat as a saint's sight removes sin; creatures vanish in the cold, as a clan is destroyed by hostility to Brahmins. Doubt and delusion depart when a true teacher is found.

With autumn clear and still no news of Sita, Rama says that if he can learn where she lives, he will conquer even Time and bring her in an instant. He laments that Sugriva, enjoying kingdom, treasury, city, and women, has forgotten his work, and threatens the arrow that killed Bali. Shiva explains that the sages understand this anger as divine play. Seeing Lakshmana enraged, Rama tells him to frighten—but bring back—their friend Sugriva.
